name: Allspice Essential Oil
partsUsed: Dried unripe berries (a leaf oil is also produced)
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried berries; pimento leaf oil is steam distilled from the leaves
aroma: Warm, sweet and spicy, like clove with a whisper of cinnamon, nutmeg and pepper.
description: Allspice oil carries the cozy, many-spiced warmth of its berries, which earned the name because they seem to taste of every spice at once. In folk magic it is a quick, energetic oil for money, luck and drive. Like clove, it is rich in eugenol and must be used sparingly on skin.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally allspice is added to money and luck oils to speed results, its fiery Mars nature lending momentum to stalled plans. A drop on a green or gold candle (rubbed in from the middle outward, well diluted) is a classic prosperity working, and it is said to add determination to spells for business success. Some practitioners use it in healing blends to bolster vitality, and its warmth makes it a welcome hearth-and-home oil in the colder months.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, allspice berry oil is used in extremely dilute massage blends (0.15% or less) to warm stiff muscles and achy joints, and in a diffuser during cold season for its comforting, spicy scent. It has a folk reputation for easing gas and a sluggish feeling digestion when massaged over the belly in a weak dilution.
dilution: Maximum 0.15% for skin (less than 1 drop per ounce of carrier, so in practice keep it to candles, charms and diffusers); avoid on the face and mucous membranes; do not use on children under 6. Diffuse sparingly, 1-2 drops at a time.
uses: Anoint green candles for money and business luck
Add a drop to a prosperity sachet or wallet charm
Diffuse with orange for a warm, welcoming home
Add one drop to a large batch of warming muscle rub (0.15% or less)
Dress a mojo bag for drive and momentum
Add to autumn and Yule simmer blends
whereToFind: Look for Pimenta dioica berry oil from Jamaica or Central America and check whether you are buying berry or leaf oil, as the leaf oil is even higher in eugenol. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: High in eugenol and contains methyleugenol: a strong skin and mucous membrane irritant and potential sensitizer, so keep skin use to 0.15% or less and never use it in the bath. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with bleeding disorders, blood-thinning medication or before surgery. Not for children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Autumn and winter suit it best, especially on a Thursday or Sunday morning when working for money and success.
interactions: Eugenol may add to the effect of anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs (such as warfarin or aspirin).
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (named by Pet Poison Helpline): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Basil Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the flowering tops and leaves
aroma: Fresh, green and sweetly herbaceous with a bright, slightly anise-like edge.
description: Basil oil captures the bright, green energy of the kitchen herb long cherished in folk magic for love, money and protection. It is a clarifying oil, often reached for when the mind feels foggy or scattered. Choose a linalool-type oil for gentler skin and aromatic use.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic basil is a herb of love and household harmony, and its oil is traditionally used to dress love and reconciliation candles or to anoint a doorframe to invite peace. It is also a favorite in money oils, especially for those who run shops, where a drop on the till or front door is said to draw customers. Basil is said to dispel confusion and fear, so it is added to blends for courage and clear decision-making.
medicalUses: Traditionally, basil oil is diffused or inhaled to lift mental fatigue, sharpen focus and ease tension headaches. Well diluted, it has a folk reputation in massage blends for tired, overworked muscles and for soothing a crampy stomach when rubbed gently over the belly.
dilution: 1% for skin (about 6 drops per ounce of carrier); avoid on the face; do not use on children under 6. Choose linalool chemotype oil rather than high-estragole types.
uses: Dress a pink or green candle for love and harmony
Anoint the shop door or cash box to draw customers
Inhale from a tissue for focus while studying
Diffuse with lemon to clear stuck energy from a room
Add to a peace and reconciliation oil blend
Blend into a dilute massage oil for tired muscles
whereToFind: Look for Ocimum basilicum ct. linalool on the label; avoid 'exotic' or high-methyl chavicol (estragole) basil where possible. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Some basil oils are high in estragole (methyl chavicol), a suspected carcinogen; high-estragole basil should be kept off the skin (Tisserand maximum 0.1%), so use only linalool-type oil on skin. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, and not for children under 6. May irritate sensitive skin. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Summer, when basil is in full leaf, and on Friday mornings for love or Thursday for money.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Bay Laurel Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the leaves
aroma: Fresh, spicy and camphoraceous, with a clean, slightly sweet medicinal edge.
description: Bay laurel oil carries the energy of the victor's wreath, long associated with achievement, prophecy and protection. It is a bright, opening oil that suits success and divination work alike. Note that it is distinct from West Indian bay (Pimenta racemosa), which smells and behaves differently.
metaphysicalUses: In folk tradition, bay is the leaf of victory and of oracles, and the oil is used to anoint candles or written petitions for success, recognition and winning a fair outcome. A drop in a diffuser before tarot or scrying is said to open prophetic insight, and many witches add it to protective and cleansing blends to clear a space before ritual. Wishes are traditionally written on bay leaves and burned; a drop of oil on the leaf is a gentle way to strengthen that working.
medicalUses: Traditionally, bay laurel oil is diffused or used in steam inhalation to clear a stuffy head during colds, and in dilute massage blends for aching muscles and stiff joints. It is also inhaled for a lift when energy and concentration flag.
dilution: Maximum 0.5% for skin (about 3 drops per ounce of carrier) because of its sensitizing potential; avoid on the face; do not use on children under 6.
uses: Anoint a gold or yellow candle for success and recognition
Dab on a bay leaf before writing and burning a wish
Diffuse before tarot or scrying for insight
Add to a protective room spray for the threshold
Inhale for confidence before an interview or exam
Blend into a dilute rub for sore muscles
whereToFind: Make sure the label says Laurus nobilis, not West Indian bay (Pimenta racemosa), which is a different oil. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Bay laurel is a known skin sensitizer: patch test and keep dilutions at 0.5% or less. It is rich in 1,8-cineole, so never apply on or near the face of infants and young children. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Not for children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Midsummer and Sundays at midday suit its solar energy best, especially for success workings.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Bergamot Essential Oil
extraction: Cold pressed from the peel; a bergapten-free (FCF) version is further processed to remove furocoumarins
aroma: Bright, sweet and citrusy with a soft floral, slightly peppery undertone, the classic scent of Earl Grey tea.
description: Bergamot oil comes from the peel of a small, sour Italian citrus, not from the North American bee balm that shares its name. It is a sunny, uplifting oil that is loved in both perfume and magic for success, money and lifting the spirits. Ordinary bergamot is strongly phototoxic, so choose a bergaptene-free (FCF) oil for anything left on the skin.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic bergamot is a money and success oil, said to draw abundance and favor, and a drop rubbed on the hands before a negotiation is a traditional charm. Its cheerful scent is used to banish gloom and restore optimism, and it works well in self-confidence blends or to anoint candles when you need to shine. Because it is gentle and light, it is a good choice for spells of peace and harmony in the home.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, bergamot is one of the most popular oils for easing nervous tension, low mood and stress, usually inhaled or diffused. It is also used in evening blends to help unwind before sleep, and in skin care for oily or blemish-prone skin (FCF oil only, well diluted).
dilution: FCF (bergaptene-free) oil: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; avoid on children under 6. Regular (non-FCF) oil: keep to 0.4% or less on skin that will see sunlight, or use only in a diffuser or wash-off products.
uses: Rub a drop of FCF blend on the palms before a business meeting
Anoint a green candle for prosperity and favor
Diffuse with lavender for a calm, cheerful home
Add to a self-confidence or glamour oil
Blend into a bedtime inhaler to unwind
Scent a money envelope or wallet charm
whereToFind: For skin use, look specifically for 'bergamot FCF' or 'bergaptene-free'. Check that it says Citrus bergamia, not Monarda (bee balm) or 'bergamot mint'. Citrus oils oxidize quickly, so buy small bottles and refrigerate. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Non-FCF bergamot is strongly phototoxic: applying it and then going into sunlight or tanning beds within 12-18 hours can cause severe burns and lasting pigmentation, so keep regular oil at 0.4% or less on exposed skin or use FCF oil. Oxidized citrus oil can irritate skin. Avoid in early pregnancy, use cautiously with children, and do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Spring and summer mornings, and Wednesdays or Sundays for success and communication.
pets: Citrus oils (limonene) are toxic to cats: never apply to pets, store out of reach, and diffuse only briefly where pets and birds can leave the room.

name: Black Pepper Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the crushed dried peppercorns; a CO2 extract is also available
aroma: Sharp, warm and spicy with a fresh, woody, slightly musky dryness.
description: Black pepper oil is a fiery, protective oil that brings courage and a sense of forward motion. Unlike the ground spice, it is surprisingly gentle and warming on skin when properly diluted. It is a favorite in protection, banishing and motivation blends.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic, pepper is a guardian, and the oil is traditionally used to dress black or red candles for protection and to drive away negativity, jealousy and unwanted attention. It is a staple ingredient in hot-foot style banishing blends and in oils for courage and mental alertness. A drop in a blend can add a kick to any working that needs speed, and it is said to strengthen boundaries.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, black pepper is used in warming massage blends for sore muscles, stiffness and cold hands and feet. It is inhaled for alertness and to curb cravings in folk smoking-cessation blends, and rubbed in dilute form over the belly for a sluggish digestion.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid the face and broken skin; do not use on children under 6.
uses: Dress a black candle for protection and banishing
Add to a boundary-setting oil for the doorway
Inhale from a tissue for courage and alertness
Blend into a warming rub for sore muscles
Add a drop to a hot-foot or 'go away' blend
Combine with ginger in a motivation diffuser blend
whereToFind: Check for Piper nigrum on the label; avoid 'pink pepper' (Schinus molle), which is a different plant. Oxidized oil is more irritating, so buy fresh and store cool. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Can irritate sensitive skin, especially when old or oxidized. Keep away from eyes. Avoid heavy use during pregnancy. Not for children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Tuesdays, during the waning moon for banishing or the waxing moon for courage, and in the colder months.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Cardamom Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried seeds; CO2 extracts are also available
aroma: Sweet, warm and spicy with a fresh, almost eucalyptus-like lift and a hint of citrus.
description: Cardamom oil is a sweet, sensual spice oil traditionally linked with love, lust and warm-hearted hospitality. It is gentler on the skin than most spice oils and blends beautifully into perfumes. Its fresh, sweet warmth makes it a favorite in romance and attraction workings.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic cardamom is an herb of love and desire, and its oil is traditionally added to love and lust oils, or used to dress red and pink candles for romance. Its clean, sweet scent is said to bring clarity to the heart and help warm a relationship that has gone cool. It is also used in welcoming blends to make guests feel at ease and in kitchen witchery for joyful gatherings.
medicalUses: Traditionally, cardamom oil is inhaled or massaged in dilution over the belly to ease nausea, bloating and indigestion. It is also diffused as a refreshing pick-me-up for mental fatigue and as a comforting scent during colds.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; avoid on children under 6 due to its 1,8-cineole content.
uses: Add to a love or attraction perfume oil
Dress a red candle for passion
Diffuse with orange to welcome guests
Rub a dilute blend over the belly after a heavy meal
Inhale from a tissue to ease travel nausea
Blend with rose for a romantic bath (in a dispersant)
whereToFind: Look for Elettaria cardamomum (green cardamom), not black cardamom (Amomum), which smells smoky and different. It is pricey, so very cheap oil is suspect. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Contains 1,8-cineole: do not apply on or near the face of infants and young children. May irritate sensitive skin. Use cautiously during pregnancy. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Fridays, especially in the evening, and during cozy autumn and winter gatherings.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Cedarwood Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the wood; Virginian is often distilled from sawmill waste
aroma: Warm, dry and woody; Atlas is softer and sweeter with a balsamic depth, while Virginian smells like a pencil shaving or cedar chest.
description: Cedarwood oil comes in two main kinds: Atlas cedar (Cedrus atlantica, a true cedar from Morocco) and Virginian cedarwood (Juniperus virginiana, actually a juniper from North America). Both are deep, grounding woods prized in magic for protection, wisdom and steady prosperity. They differ in scent and chemistry, so note which one a recipe calls for.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, cedar is a tree of strength and sacred space, and its oil is used to anoint ritual tools, altars and doorframes for protection and purification. Its grounding scent is used in meditation to steady the mind and connect with ancestral wisdom. It is also a classic oil for slow, lasting prosperity, often added to money blends to give them staying power, and a drop in a dream pillow is said to keep away nightmares.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, cedarwood is diffused or used in bedtime blends for its calming, sleep-supporting scent and to ease nervous tension. It is a long-standing ingredient in hair and scalp care for oily scalp and dandruff, and in skin blends for oily or blemish-prone skin. Atlas cedar is also inhaled for a congested chest.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face and scalp blends; for children over 6, keep to 0.5-1%.
uses: Anoint an altar or ritual tools for consecration
Add to a protection oil for doors and windows
Diffuse at bedtime or add to a dream pillow
Blend into a grounding meditation roller
Add to money oils for lasting prosperity
Mix into a scalp oil with rosemary
whereToFind: Check the Latin name to know whether you have Atlas (Cedrus atlantica) or Virginian (Juniperus virginiana); 'Texas cedarwood' is Juniperus ashei. Avoid 'cedar leaf' oil (Thuja), which is high in toxic thujone. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding as a precaution. Can irritate very sensitive skin. Do not confuse with cedar leaf (Thuja) oil, which is neurotoxic. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Winter and late autumn, and Thursday evenings for prosperity or at dusk for protection and grounding.
pets: Use cautiously around cats and birds; never diffuse in a closed room with pets.

name: Cinnamon Essential Oil
partsUsed: Leaves (leaf oil) or inner bark (bark oil)
extraction: Steam distilled, either from the leaves and twigs or from the dried inner bark
aroma: Leaf oil is warm, spicy and clove-like; bark oil is intensely sweet, rich and true to the cinnamon stick.
description: Cinnamon oil comes in two very different forms. Leaf oil is high in eugenol and is the more practical choice for magic and diffusing, while bark oil is rich in cinnamaldehyde and is a strong skin irritant and sensitizer that should almost never touch the skin. Both carry the fiery, solar energy of the spice that has drawn money and love for centuries.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic cinnamon is a powerhouse of quick success, money and attraction. A single drop of well-diluted leaf oil is traditionally added to money drawing and road opener blends, or used to dress gold and red candles. It is said to raise spiritual vibrations and sharpen psychic focus when diffused, and it is an old ingredient in love and lust oils to bring heat and passion. Many witches dress candles with oil rather than applying it to the body, which is the safer approach.
medicalUses: Traditionally, cinnamon leaf oil is diffused in small amounts during cold and flu season for its warming, comforting scent and its reputation for freshening the air. Very dilute leaf oil appears in folk warming rubs for cold extremities and stiff muscles. Bark oil is generally reserved for diffusion or left alone in home use.
dilution: Leaf oil: maximum 0.5% (about 3 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; never on the face. Bark oil: no more than 0.07% on skin (well under 1 drop per ounce), so in practice do not apply bark oil to skin at all. Neither oil should be used on children under 6.
uses: Dress a gold candle for fast money (diluted leaf oil)
Add one drop to a road opener or success oil
Diffuse with orange and clove in winter
Anoint a red candle for passion and attraction
Add to a prosperity floor wash in tiny amounts
Scent a money bowl or jar spell
whereToFind: Check whether the label says leaf or bark, and look for Cinnamomum verum (Ceylon) rather than cassia (Cinnamomum cassia), which is harsher. Bark oil is much more expensive than leaf oil. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Cinnamon bark oil is a strong skin irritant and sensitizer: it can cause burning, redness and lasting allergic reactions even at low dilution, so keep it off the skin entirely. Leaf oil is high in eugenol and also irritates skin and mucous membranes. Avoid both in pregnancy, breastfeeding, with blood thinners, before surgery and with children. Never swallow, and keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Sundays at sunrise or noon for success, and the dark half of the year, especially around Yule.
interactions: Eugenol (leaf oil) may add to the effect of anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs.
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (named by Pet Poison Helpline): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Citronella Essential Oil
partsUsed: Leaves and stems of the grass
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh or partly dried grass
aroma: Fresh, lemony and grassy with a sweet, slightly woody undertone.
description: Citronella oil is the familiar summer porch scent, distilled from a tall tropical grass related to lemongrass. In folk magic it is a cleansing, repelling oil, used to send away unwanted influences just as it is used to send away insects. Java citronella is generally considered the finer, sweeter type.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, citronella is used to cleanse and freshen a space and to repel unwanted energies, gossip and pests of every kind. It is added to floor washes and room sprays to clear stale or heavy atmospheres, and to protection blends for summer gatherings outdoors. Its bright scent is also said to lift the spirits and encourage clear, cheerful thinking.
medicalUses: In traditional and modern home use, citronella is best known as a natural insect repellent in candles, diffusers and very dilute body sprays. It is also diffused to refresh the mind and mask musty odors.
dilution: Up to 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid the face; do not use on children under 6. Reapply repellent blends often rather than increasing the strength.
uses: Burn citronella candles to cleanse an outdoor ritual space
Add to a floor wash to clear stale energy
Make a dilute repellent spray for summer evenings
Diffuse to freshen a musty room
Add to a protection blend for camping or travel
whereToFind: Check for Cymbopogon winterianus or C. nardus on the label. Many 'citronella' candles and torches use synthetic fragrance, so buy the pure oil separately if you want the real thing. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Can irritate or sensitize skin, especially when oxidized; patch test. Avoid during pregnancy. Not for children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: High summer, especially on warm evenings and at sunset when gathering outdoors.
pets: Keep away from cats and dogs; never use citronella products on pets.

name: Clary Sage Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the flowering tops and leaves
aroma: Herbaceous, sweet and nutty with a soft, musky, almost wine-like depth.
description: Clary sage oil is a dreamy, lunar oil once known as 'clear eye' for its folk use in soothing the eyes. It is different from common garden sage and is far gentler, lacking sage's high thujone content. Witches value it for dreamwork, intuition and calm.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, clary sage is used to deepen dreams, open intuition and bring clear vision. A drop on a pillowcase or in a dream oil is said to encourage vivid, meaningful dreams, and it is diffused before divination, scrying or moon rituals. Its soothing nature makes it a favorite in blends for calm, emotional balance and gentle euphoria, and it is often connected with women's mysteries and moon cycles.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, clary sage is one of the most commonly used oils for menstrual discomfort, applied well diluted as an abdominal massage. It is also diffused or inhaled to ease stress, tension and restlessness at bedtime, and used in massage for tight muscles.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; for children over 6, 0.5-1%.
uses: Add a drop to a dream pillow or dream oil
Diffuse before tarot, scrying or a Full Moon rite
Rub a dilute blend on the belly for menstrual cramps
Blend with lavender in a bedtime roller
Anoint a silver or white candle for intuition
Add to a calming bath (in a dispersant)
whereToFind: Look for Salvia sclarea, and do not substitute common sage (Salvia officinalis), which is a much stronger, riskier oil. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Avoid during pregnancy (except under professional care at term), as it is traditionally thought to influence hormones and the uterus. Avoid with estrogen-sensitive conditions. It can make some people drowsy, so avoid combining it with alcohol or driving after heavy use. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Monday evenings and nights of the Full Moon, ideally just before sleep.
interactions: Traditionally cautioned with alcohol and sedatives because of possible added drowsiness.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Clove Essential Oil
partsUsed: Flower buds (leaf and stem oils also exist)
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried flower buds
aroma: Hot, sweet and spicy, deeply warm, woody and unmistakably like the whole spice.
description: Clove oil is a potent, warming spice oil long associated with protection, banishing and drawing money. It is rich in eugenol, which gives it its numbing traditional reputation but also makes it a significant skin irritant. Use it as an accent, a single drop goes a long way.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic clove is used to stop gossip, protect the home and drive away hostile forces, and the oil is traditionally used to dress black or purple candles for banishing and protection. It also appears in money and success blends to add heat and draw riches, and in love oils to attract and bind affection. Some practitioners use it to purify and raise the energy of a space before ritual.
medicalUses: Clove bud oil has a very old folk reputation for numbing toothache, traditionally applied in tiny, heavily diluted amounts on a cotton swab while waiting to see a dentist. It is also used in very dilute warming massage blends and diffused in winter for its comforting, air-freshening scent.
dilution: Maximum 0.5% (about 3 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; never on the face, and never undiluted on skin, gums or mucous membranes; do not use on children under 6. Choose bud oil over leaf or stem oil.
uses: Dress a black candle to stop gossip
Add to a protection oil for the front door
Anoint a green candle with clove and orange for money
Diffuse with orange and cinnamon in winter
Add to a pomander-inspired protection charm
Adults only: a heavily diluted dab for temporary tooth discomfort while waiting for the dentist (do not swallow)
whereToFind: Choose clove bud oil (Syzygium aromaticum), which is gentler than leaf or stem oil. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: High in eugenol: a strong skin and mucous membrane irritant and sensitizer that can damage gum tissue if used too strong. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with bleeding disorders, blood-thinning medication or before surgery. Not for children, and never put clove oil in a baby's mouth for teething. Do not swallow; swallowed clove oil is dangerous for children. For toothache use only a heavily diluted dab as an adult and see a dentist.
bestTime: Thursdays for money and Saturdays for protection and banishing, especially in late autumn and winter.
interactions: Eugenol may add to the effect of anticoagulant and antiplatelet drugs (such as warfarin or aspirin).
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (named by Pet Poison Helpline): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Cypress Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the needles and young twigs
aroma: Fresh, clean and evergreen with a dry, slightly smoky, resinous woodiness.
description: Cypress oil carries the solemn, evergreen energy of the tree long planted in cemeteries as a symbol of eternity and passage. It is a comforting oil in times of grief and change, and a strong ally in protection and ancestor work. Its fresh scent is also deeply cleansing.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, cypress is a tree of death, rebirth and the eternal, and its oil is used in rituals of mourning, transition and honoring the dead. It is said to ease grief and help release what has ended so that new growth can come. Witches add it to protection and blessing oils, to anoint ancestor altars, and to bring steadiness and strength during upheaval. It is also traditional in Samhain workings.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, cypress is used in steam or diffusion for coughs and congestion, and in dilute massage blends for tired, heavy legs and sluggish circulation. It is also diffused to bring calm and composure in times of stress and sorrow.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; for children over 6, 0.5-1%. Use fresh oil, as oxidized cypress is more irritating.
uses: Anoint an ancestor altar or memorial candle
Diffuse during grief or times of transition
Add to a protection oil for the home
Use in a Samhain ritual blend
Blend into a leg massage oil for tired legs
Add to a steam inhalation for coughs
whereToFind: Check for Cupressus sempervirens; other cypress species and 'blue cypress' (Callitris) are different oils. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Generally gentle, but oxidized oil can irritate skin, so store cool and tightly capped. Avoid during pregnancy as a precaution. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Late autumn, especially around Samhain, and on Saturdays at dusk.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Eucalyptus Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh or partly dried leaves
aroma: Sharp, cool and camphoraceous, intensely fresh and clean with a medicinal, minty edge.
description: Eucalyptus oil is the classic healing and clearing oil, instantly recognizable from cold season remedies. In folk magic it is used for purification and for health and protection spells. Eucalyptus radiata is a softer, gentler alternative to globulus for sensitive noses.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, eucalyptus is a healing oil, used to anoint blue candles for good health and recovery and added to healing poppets or sachets. It is a strong purifier, diffused to clear the energy of a sickroom or a space after an argument, and is said to break up stagnant or stuck energy. Some practitioners add it to protection blends to keep illness and negativity at bay.
medicalUses: In traditional and modern aromatherapy, eucalyptus is widely used in steam inhalation, chest rubs and diffusers to ease congestion, coughs and the misery of colds. It is also used in dilute massage blends for aching muscles and inhaled to clear a tension headache.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid the face. Do not use on or near the face of children under 10 because of its high 1,8-cineole content; choose a gentler alternative for little ones.
uses: Anoint a blue candle for healing and recovery
Diffuse in a sickroom to clear heavy energy
Add to a steam bowl for congestion (adults)
Hang eucalyptus in the shower with a drop of oil
Add to a cleansing floor wash
Blend into a chest rub for adults
whereToFind: Check whether you have Eucalyptus globulus (strong) or E. radiata (gentler). Lemon eucalyptus (Corymbia citriodora) is a different oil with a different use. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: High in 1,8-cineole: never apply on or near the face of infants and young children, as it can cause breathing problems. Highly toxic if swallowed: even small amounts can cause seizures, especially in children, so store it locked away and call Poison Control (1-800-222-1222) after any swallowing. Avoid with epilepsy.
bestTime: Winter and early spring, during cold season, and on Monday evenings for healing work.
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (named by Pet Poison Helpline): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Frankincense Essential Oil
latin: Boswellia sacra; Boswellia carterii (also B. serrata, B. frereana)
extraction: Steam distilled from the oleo-gum resin; CO2 extracts are also available
aroma: Warm, resinous and balsamic with a fresh, peppery-citrus top and a soft, sacred woody depth.
description: Frankincense oil is the oil of the temple, distilled from the resin tears of trees that have been burned as offerings for thousands of years. It is one of the most versatile oils in magic, raising energy for meditation, consecration, protection and spirit work. It is gentle on the skin and blends with nearly everything.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, frankincense is used to consecrate altars, tools, candles and sacred space, and to anoint the brow before meditation or prayer. It is said to raise vibrations, deepen spiritual connection and invite divine presence, making it a fitting offering for many deities. Witches also use it for protection, exorcism of negativity, and in success blends, where its solar quality is said to bring blessings and recognition.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, frankincense is diffused to slow and deepen the breath, calming anxiety and supporting meditation. It is used in skin care for mature, dry or scarred skin, and in steam inhalation or chest rubs to ease coughs and congestion.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; for children over 6, 0.5-1%. Gentle, but always dilute.
uses: Consecrate an altar, wand or new tools
Anoint the brow before meditation or prayer
Diffuse during ritual to raise sacred energy
Add to protection and blessing oils
Blend into a face oil for mature skin
Dress a white or gold candle as an offering
whereToFind: Frankincense is often adulterated and some species are over-harvested, so look for ethically sourced oil that names the species (Boswellia sacra, carterii, serrata or frereana). Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Generally gentle, but oxidized oil can irritate skin, so store cool and tightly capped. Avoid in early pregnancy as a precaution. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Sunrise and Sundays, at any time of year, and especially at the solstices and on sabbats.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Ginger Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried or fresh rhizome; CO2 extracts are also available
aroma: Warm, spicy and earthy with a sharp, lemony freshness and a woody bite.
description: Ginger oil is a fiery, energizing oil that brings speed and power to spellwork. In folk magic it is used to give a boost to love, money and success, and to fan the flames of passion. It is also a cherished traditional aid for nausea and aching muscles.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, ginger is added to spells to make them work faster and with more force, and the oil is used to dress candles for money, success and passion. It is said to bring courage and confidence and to warm up a stalled relationship or project. A drop in a love or lust oil adds heat, and it is used in healing workings to support strength and vitality.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy, ginger oil is inhaled from a tissue or inhaler to ease nausea and motion sickness, and massaged in dilution over the belly for indigestion. It is a classic warming oil in massage blends for sore muscles, stiff joints and cold hands and feet.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid the face; for children over 6, 0.5-1%. Fresh ginger CO2 is more potent than distilled oil.
uses: Add a drop to any spell oil to speed results
Dress a red candle for passion
Inhale from a tissue for travel nausea
Blend into a warming muscle rub
Anoint a green candle with orange and ginger for money
Add to a courage or confidence roller
whereToFind: Look for Zingiber officinale; note whether the oil is from dried or fresh root, as the scents differ. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Can irritate sensitive skin, especially when oxidized. Use cautiously during pregnancy and consult a professional before using for morning sickness. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Tuesdays and Sundays, and autumn and winter when its warmth is most welcome.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Honeysuckle Essential Oil
extraction: True honeysuckle is solvent-extracted as a rare absolute (or as a CO2 or enfleurage extract); it cannot be practically steam distilled
aroma: Sweet, honeyed and heady, a lush, nectar-like floral with a soft green edge.
description: True honeysuckle oil is rare: it is produced only in tiny quantities as a costly absolute, and almost everything sold as 'honeysuckle oil' is a synthetic fragrance oil or a blend. Both carry the sweet, nostalgic scent of summer hedgerows. In folk magic honeysuckle is tied to prosperity, psychic sight and sweet affection.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, honeysuckle is a flower of luck, money and sweetness, and its scent is used to dress candles for prosperity and to draw friendship and love. Folk tradition says crushing the flowers and touching them to the brow heightens psychic ability, so the oil is used in a similar way in intuition blends. It is also used to sweeten a relationship, recall happy memories and invite peace into the home. For magical work, a well-made infused oil or a fragrance oil used only on candles and charms can carry the same intention.
medicalUses: True honeysuckle absolute is used in perfumery more than therapy. In traditional aromatherapy its sweet scent is inhaled or worn as perfume to lift the mood, soothe stress and bring a sense of comfort and nostalgia. Fragrance oils have no aromatherapy value and should not be used therapeutically.
dilution: Absolute: 0.5-1% (3-6 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin as a perfume; avoid on children under 6. Fragrance oils should not be applied to skin unless labeled skin-safe, and are best kept to candles, sachets and charms.
uses: Dress a green candle for prosperity and luck
Anoint the brow area (diluted absolute) for intuition
Add to a sweetening jar spell
Wear a dilute absolute perfume for attraction
Scent a friendship or love sachet
Use fragrance oil on candles and charms only
whereToFind: Expect real honeysuckle absolute to be very expensive and sold in tiny amounts from specialist perfumery suppliers. Anything cheap labeled 'honeysuckle essential oil' is almost certainly a fragrance oil. You can also make a simple infused oil from fresh flowers in a carrier oil. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Absolutes may contain traces of solvent and can sensitize skin; patch test. Fragrance oils are synthetic, may irritate skin and must never be diffused for therapy or swallowed. Honeysuckle berries are toxic, so keep the plant and its products away from children and pets. Avoid during pregnancy.
bestTime: Early summer evenings, when honeysuckle blooms and its scent is strongest at dusk, and on Thursdays for prosperity.
pets: Keep the oil, fragrance oil and honeysuckle berries away from cats, dogs and birds.

name: Hyssop Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the leaves and flowering tops
aroma: Sweet, warm and herbaceous with a camphoraceous, slightly spicy freshness.
description: Hyssop has been one of the great herbs of spiritual cleansing and purification for millennia, and its oil carries that reputation. It is also one of the more hazardous essential oils, because some types are high in pinocamphone, which can trigger seizures. Many witches prefer working with the dried herb, or with hyssop var. decumbens oil, which is gentler.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally, hyssop is used to cleanse people, objects and spaces of negativity, guilt and spiritual heaviness. A drop of oil is added to a cleansing bath (properly dispersed) or floor wash, or used to purify ritual tools and candles before use. It is also said to protect against harmful magic and is used in healing spells to clear the way for recovery.
medicalUses: Hyssop has a long folk history as a remedy for coughs and chest complaints. In traditional aromatherapy the oil is used sparingly, mostly in very dilute chest rubs or short inhalations, and many aromatherapists now favor safer oils for the same purpose.
dilution: Maximum 0.3% (about 2 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin for standard (pinocamphone) hyssop. Never use on children, and choose Hyssopus officinalis var. decumbens (linalool type) where possible. Diffuse only briefly, if at all.
uses: Add a drop to a spiritual cleansing floor wash
Purify ritual tools and altar cloths
Dress a white candle for cleansing and release
Add to a protection oil against harmful influences
Mist a dilute cleansing spray around the ritual space (adults only, not on skin)
whereToFind: Check whether the oil is standard Hyssopus officinalis (high in pinocamphone) or var. decumbens (linalool-rich and gentler). It is not widely sold, so buy only from a specialist. Buy from a reputable aromatherapy supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin and extraction method on the label. Pure oil comes in dark amber or cobalt glass with a dropper cap. Avoid anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil', and be wary of prices that seem too good to be true.
caution: Standard hyssop oil contains pinocamphone, a convulsant: keep skin use to 0.3% or less, and never use it with epilepsy or a seizure history, during pregnancy or breastfeeding, or on children. Never swallow; seizures have been reported after ingestion. Do not use with high fever. When in doubt, use the dried herb or the linalool type (var. decumbens) instead.
bestTime: Early spring for seasonal cleansing, and Saturday mornings or any time before a major ritual.
interactions: Avoid with seizure-threshold-lowering conditions and use caution alongside anticonvulsant medication.
pets: Keep well away from pets; never diffuse around cats, dogs or birds.

name: Jasmine Essential Oil
partsUsed: Freshly picked flowers, gathered at night or dawn when the scent is strongest
extraction: Solvent-extracted absolute: the blossoms are first made into a waxy concrete, which is washed with alcohol to yield the absolute; true steam distillation is rarely possible, though CO2 extracts and traditional attar (distilled into sandalwood) also exist
aroma: Heady, honeyed and narcotic, with a warm animalic depth and a faintly fruity, green edge.
description: Jasmine is the night-blooming queen of the perfumer's garden, so precious that thousands of hand-picked blossoms go into a single small vial. Because the flowers are too delicate for steam, what you buy is almost always an absolute rather than a distilled oil. In folk magic it is a moon flower through and through, linked to love, dreams and the sweetness of night.
metaphysicalUses: Jasmine is traditionally worked for spiritual love and soulful romance rather than quick attraction, and a single drop on a pink or white candle is said to call in tenderness. Its moon rulership makes it a favorite for dream work, prophetic dreams and opening intuition, often blended into a pillow mist or anointed on the third eye in a well-diluted oil. In folk practice it is also used to draw abundance and to restore self-worth, and many witches wear it to full moon rites as a perfume of devotion.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy jasmine is valued as an emotional oil: its scent is used to lift heaviness, soothe nervous tension and support a sense of confidence and sensuality. It has a long folk use in skin care for dry or mature skin, usually in tiny amounts, and is sometimes added to massage blends for menstrual or labor comfort under the guidance of a qualified practitioner. Most of its value is in inhalation, where a drop or two goes a long way.
dilution: 0.5-1% (3-6 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 0.5% or less for face; it is intensely strong, so one drop is often enough. Avoid on children under 6.
uses: Anoint a pink candle for self-love
Add one drop to a dream pillow or night mist
Wear as a diluted perfume for full moon rites
Blend with sandalwood for a devotional anointing oil
Scent love letters or a romance sachet
Inhale from a tissue during low or anxious moods
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Real jasmine absolute is expensive, so suspiciously cheap 'jasmine oil' is almost always synthetic or heavily cut. Many reputable sellers offer it pre-diluted (3-10% in jojoba), which is a good, honest way to buy it. Ask whether it is grandiflorum or sambac, as they smell quite different.
caution: Absolutes can contain traces of extraction solvent and jasmine is a moderate skin sensitizer, so patch test and keep dilutions low. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy until labor. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children. Do not diffuse continuously in small rooms, as the scent can cause headaches.
bestTime: Work with jasmine after dusk, ideally in high summer when the vines bloom, and especially on Monday nights under the full moon.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Juniper Berry Essential Oil
partsUsed: Ripe, dried or partially dried berries (actually fleshy cones)
extraction: Steam distilled from the crushed berries; 'juniper' oils distilled from needles and twigs are a cheaper, different product
aroma: Crisp, resinous and woody, with a peppery, faintly fruity gin-like brightness.
description: Juniper has been burned to purify homes, temples and sickrooms across Europe for centuries, and the essential oil carries that same clean, fierce energy in a bottle. Distilled from the berries, it smells like a cold forest morning with a splash of gin. In folk magic it is one of the great protectors and purifiers.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic juniper is used to drive out unwanted energies and to protect a home from theft, accidents and ill intent. A few drops in a spray bottle of water and alcohol makes a quick cleansing mist for doorways and thresholds, and it is a classic addition to banishing and uncrossing oils. Traditionally it is also linked to masculine vitality and to clearing the mind before divination or important decisions.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy juniper berry is used as a warming, detoxifying oil, added to massage blends for stiff joints, rheumatic aches and tired muscles. It has a folk reputation for helping with fluid retention and sluggish circulation, and it is sometimes used in steam inhalations during colds. Emotionally it is used to clear mental clutter and restore a sense of purpose.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face. Avoid on children under 6.
uses: Mist thresholds and windows for home protection
Add to a banishing or uncrossing oil
Diffuse after an argument or illness to clear the air
Anoint a black or red candle for protection
Blend into a warming massage oil for sore muscles
Add a drop to a cleansing floor wash
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Look specifically for 'juniper berry' (Juniperus communis fructus) rather than 'juniper' or 'juniper twig', and buy small bottles, since the oil oxidizes fairly quickly once opened.
caution: Oxidized juniper oil can irritate or sensitize skin, so store it cool, tightly capped and use within a year or two. Traditionally avoided during pregnancy and by people with kidney disease. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Juniper is strongest in late autumn and winter, when the berries ripen and the dark half of the year calls for protection and cleansing.
pets: Do not diffuse around cats, birds or small animals.

name: Lavender Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh flowering tops
aroma: Clean, sweet and floral with soft herbaceous and faintly woody undertones.
description: Lavender is the most beloved and versatile oil in the cabinet, gentle enough for beginners yet useful in almost every kind of work. True lavender, Lavandula angustifolia, is softer and sweeter than its camphoraceous cousins lavandin and spike lavender. In folk magic it is a herb of peace, love, purification and restful sleep.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally lavender is used to calm a tense home, invite restful sleep and peaceful dreams, and soften the energy around grief or conflict. It is a classic ingredient in love and reconciliation oils, and a few drops in a ritual bath are said to cleanse the aura and draw gentle, kind love. Many witches use it to anoint candles for healing work, to bless children's rooms with a well-diluted mist, and as an all-purpose substitute when another floral oil is not on hand.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy lavender is the go-to oil for nervous tension, restlessness and trouble falling asleep, usually by inhalation or a drop on the pillow. It has a long folk use for soothing minor burns, insect bites and small scrapes once diluted, and for easing tension headaches when massaged into the temples and neck in a carrier. It is also added to massage blends for sore muscles and to bath oils for general relaxation.
dilution: 1-3% (6-18 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; 0.5-1% for children over 2. Avoid on infants under 3 months.
uses: Mist pillows and bed linens for peaceful sleep
Add to a ritual cleansing bath
Anoint a blue or lavender candle for healing
Blend into a love or reconciliation oil
Diffuse during meditation or after a stressful day
Add to a smoke cleansing alternative spray
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Check that it says Lavandula angustifolia, not lavandin (L. x intermedia) or spike lavender (L. latifolia), which are cheaper and more camphoraceous. High-altitude French, Bulgarian and English lavenders are well regarded. Lavender is one of the most frequently adulterated oils, so a trusted supplier matters.
caution: Generally one of the gentlest oils, but oxidized lavender can cause skin sensitization or allergic reactions, so keep it fresh and capped and patch test. A few cases of breast tissue swelling in children using lavender products have been reported, though a link is unproven; use moderately with children. Swallowed lavender has made toddlers drowsy and confused, so keep the bottle out of reach.
bestTime: Lavender is at its peak in midsummer when the fields bloom, and it is best used in the evening hours for sleep, peace and dream work.
interactions: May add to the effect of sedative drugs and herbs; mention it before surgery.
pets: Lavender is listed as toxic to cats; diffuse only in rooms pets can leave and never apply to pets.

name: Lemon Essential Oil
extraction: Cold pressed (expressed) from the fresh peel; a steam distilled version also exists and is not phototoxic
aroma: Bright, sharp and sunny, exactly like freshly zested lemon peel.
description: Lemon oil is pure sunshine in a bottle, pressed straight from the zest. It is the classic cleansing oil of the kitchen witch, used to clear both grime and stale energy. Like most citrus oils it is bright and uplifting, but it fades quickly and must be handled with care in sunlight.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic lemon is a cleanser of the highest order, added to floor washes and spray mists to strip away lingering negativity, especially after illness, arguments or a move into a new home. It is traditionally used to cleanse crystals and tools, to sharpen focus during study, and to bring freshness to friendship and love spells. Its lunar rulership makes it fitting for full moon cleansing and for clearing the slate at the end of a cycle.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy lemon is used to refresh and uplift the mind, ease mental fatigue and lift low spirits, mainly through diffusion or inhalation. It is a common addition to steam inhalations and diffuser blends during colds, and many people find a whiff of lemon helpful for mild nausea and travel sickness. It also has a folk use in household cleaners for its fresh scent.
dilution: Cold pressed lemon: maximum 2% (about 12 drops per ounce) on skin that will be exposed to sun, or keep skin covered from sun and UV for 12 hours; 1% for face. Steam distilled lemon is not phototoxic. Avoid on children under 2.
uses: Add to a cleansing floor wash
Diffuse during study or exams for focus
Make a cleansing spray for a new home
Cleanse altar tools with a lemon-water wipe
Blend into a friendship or happy home oil
Inhale from a tissue for travel nausea
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Choose organic lemon when possible, since pesticides concentrate in the peel. Citrus oils oxidize quickly, so buy small amounts, store in the fridge and use within about a year.
caution: Cold pressed lemon is phototoxic: above 2% on skin that then sees sun or tanning beds within 12 hours, it can cause burns and dark patches. Oxidized citrus oil can sensitize the skin. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children. Can damage some plastics and finished surfaces.
bestTime: Lemon is best used in the bright morning hours and in late winter and spring, when homes need a fresh cleansing.
pets: Citrus oils (limonene) are toxic to cats: never apply to pets, store out of reach, and diffuse only briefly where pets and birds can leave the room.

name: Lemon Balm (Melissa) Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh leaves and flowering tops; the yield is extremely low, which makes true melissa oil very costly
aroma: Soft, sweet and lemony with a green, honeyed, herbaceous heart.
description: Melissa takes its name from the Greek for honeybee, and bees adore the plant as much as herbalists always have. Its essential oil is one of the rarest and most precious in aromatherapy, since tons of leaves yield only a little oil. In folk magic it is a herb of joy, healing and gentle love.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally melissa is used to mend a heavy heart, attract love and friendship, and bring cheer to a sad or anxious household. It is a lovely oil for healing spells, especially those aimed at emotional recovery after loss, and for blessing new friendships. In folk practice it is also linked to success and to honoring the bees, making it a fitting offering-scent for garden and pollinator magic.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy melissa is prized as a calming, uplifting oil for anxiety, grief, restlessness and nervous sleeplessness, mostly by inhalation. It has a folk reputation for helping with cold sores when used in a very low dilution, and it is used in tiny amounts in blends for emotional shock and overwhelm.
dilution: Maximum 0.9% (about 5 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 0.5% for face. Avoid on children under 6. Diffuse sparingly.
uses: Diffuse to lift a grieving or anxious home
Anoint a yellow candle for joy
Add to a friendship or reconciliation oil
Blend with rose for heart-healing work
Scent an offering for bee and garden magic
Inhale from a tissue during overwhelm
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Melissa is one of the most adulterated oils on the market, often 'stretched' with lemongrass, citronella or lemon. Genuine melissa is expensive; a cheap bottle is almost certainly not the real thing. Buying it pre-diluted in jojoba from a reputable distiller is a sensible choice.
caution: High in citral, so it can sensitize skin; keep dilutions low (0.9% or less) and patch test. Avoid on damaged, inflamed or very sensitive skin and on children under 6. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy. Use with caution if you have glaucoma or take diabetes medication. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Melissa is happiest in early summer, just before the plant flowers, and in sunny morning hours when the bees are busy.
interactions: Citral-rich oils are cautioned with diabetes medication (mainly with oral use).
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Lemongrass Essential Oil
latin: Cymbopogon citratus (West Indian); Cymbopogon flexuosus (East Indian)
partsUsed: Fresh or partly dried grass blades
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh or partially dried leaves
aroma: Sharp, zesty and lemony, with a grassy, earthy sweetness underneath.
description: Lemongrass is a powerful, punchy oil with a bright citrus scent that cuts through stagnation in a room or a spell. It is the backbone of the famous Van Van oil of Southern folk magic, used to clear away crossed conditions and open the road. Strong and inexpensive, it should still be used sparingly.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic lemongrass is used to cleanse away bad luck, break hexes and open blocked paths, and it is the defining scent of Van Van oil. It is traditionally worked into floor washes and spiritual baths to clear a home or business of stuck energy, and planted or scented around the home to repel snakes and unwanted visitors. It is also used to sharpen psychic awareness and to stir up lust and passion in partner work.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy lemongrass is used in massage blends for tired, achy muscles and as an energizing scent for mental fatigue. It has a long folk use as a natural insect repellent and room deodorizer, and it appears in small amounts in skin care for oily skin. Inhaled, it is used to sharpen focus and banish sluggishness.
dilution: Maximum 0.7% (about 4 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid on the face. Avoid on children under 6.
uses: Make a Van Van style road-opening oil
Add to an uncrossing floor wash
Anoint a candle to break a streak of bad luck
Diffuse to clear stagnant energy in a workspace
Add to an outdoor insect-repelling spray
Blend into a warming oil for tired legs
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Lemongrass is affordable and widely available; check which species you are buying, as the two smell slightly different. Buy small bottles and store cool, since citral-rich oils oxidize.
caution: High in citral, which is a known skin sensitizer and irritant; keep dilutions at 0.7% or less and never use neat. Avoid in pregnancy and on damaged skin. Cautioned in glaucoma. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Use lemongrass in the morning hours or on Wednesdays for road opening, and in late summer when the grass is lush and fragrant.
interactions: Citral-rich oils are cautioned with diabetes medication (mainly with oral use).
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs if licked or used heavily; never apply to pets.

name: Myrrh Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the gum resin; CO2 extracts and resinoids are also sold
aroma: Warm, earthy and bittersweet, with a smoky, slightly medicinal balsamic depth.
description: Myrrh is one of the oldest sacred aromatics in the world, offered in temples of Egypt and Mesopotamia and used to embalm the honored dead. Its oil is thick, dark and slow, the scent of deep ritual and sorrow transformed. In magic it is frankincense's lunar partner, pairing beautifully for consecration and spiritual work.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally myrrh is used to consecrate altars, tools and amulets, and to deepen meditation and spiritual focus. Paired with frankincense, it forms a classic blessing and purification blend. In folk magic it is also worked into protection oils, banishing rites and funerary or ancestor rituals, where it is said to honor the dead and carry prayers. Because it is ruled by the Moon, many witches use it to empower lunar rites and to strengthen spells cast by other oils.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy myrrh is valued for skin care, especially dry, cracked or mature skin, and for folk use on minor wounds once diluted. It has a very old reputation as a mouth and gum remedy, and is used in chest rubs and inhalations for coughs and congestion. Emotionally it is used to calm, steady and support people through grief.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face. Avoid on children under 6.
uses: Consecrate altar tools and jewelry
Blend with frankincense for a blessing oil
Anoint candles for ancestor and grief rites
Add to a protection or banishing oil
Scent a meditation space before trance work
Blend into a rich balm for dry hands
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Myrrh oil is thick and may need warming in your hands to pour. Look for Commiphora myrrha from Somalia, Ethiopia or Kenya, and favor suppliers who discuss sustainable, fair harvesting of the resin.
caution: Traditionally avoided throughout pregnancy and while breastfeeding. Can occasionally irritate sensitive skin; patch test. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children. Myrrh tincture's old mouthwash use does not apply to the essential oil.
bestTime: Myrrh suits the dark half of the year, especially Samhain through midwinter, and is best worked at night.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Nutmeg Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried, ground seeds; mace oil is distilled from the red aril around the seed
aroma: Warm, sweet and spicy with a soft woody, slightly peppery edge.
description: Nutmeg oil smells like holiday baking with a mysterious, heady depth. In folk magic the whole nut is carried for luck and fidelity, and the oil is used for prosperity, good fortune and psychic opening. It is potent and should be used in small amounts.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally nutmeg is used to attract money and good fortune, and a drop on a green candle or in a wallet sachet oil is a classic gambler's charm. In folk practice it is also worked for fidelity in relationships and for health and protection on journeys. Its warm, slightly intoxicating scent is used in small amounts to open psychic awareness before divination, often blended with other spice oils in prosperity mixtures.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy nutmeg is a warming oil used in massage blends for aching joints, stiff muscles and cold hands and feet. It has a folk use in abdominal massage blends for sluggish digestion, and its scent is used to revive and energize during mental fatigue. It is always used in small proportions.
dilution: Maximum 0.8% (about 5 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid on the face. Avoid on children under 6.
uses: Anoint a green candle for money drawing
Add a drop to a prosperity or gambler's oil
Blend with orange and clove for a warm home oil
Scent a fidelity charm bag
Diffuse a tiny amount before divination
Add to a warming massage oil for cold hands
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Nutmeg oil from Indonesia (East Indian) and Grenada (West Indian) differ slightly in scent. Choose a supplier who lists the myristicin content or provides a GC/MS report.
caution: Contains myristicin and safrole, which are psychoactive and toxic in quantity; swallowing the oil can cause hallucinations, nausea, rapid heartbeat and poisoning. Never take internally. Avoid in pregnancy, while breastfeeding, and in epilepsy. Keep skin use at 0.8% or less. Keep well away from children.
bestTime: Nutmeg belongs to late autumn and winter, the season of spice and hearth, and is best used on Thursdays for Jupiter's luck and prosperity.
pets: Keep well away from cats and dogs; never apply to pets.

name: Palmarosa Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried or fresh grass, usually just before flowering
aroma: Soft, sweet and rosy with a fresh, lemony grass note.
description: Palmarosa is a grass that smells surprisingly like roses, making it a gentle, affordable heart oil for everyday love and healing work. It was once shipped from India as 'Turkish geranium' and used to stretch rose oil. Kind to the skin and lovely in blends, it deserves far more use than it gets.
metaphysicalUses: In modern folk practice palmarosa is used as an accessible stand-in for rose in love, friendship and self-love work, and a drop on a pink candle invites warmth and affection. It is a soothing choice for heart healing after a breakup or loss, and for blessing new relationships and friendships. Its gentle, steady nature also makes it useful for calming spells and peaceful home blends.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy palmarosa is especially valued in skin care, used for balancing both dry and oily skin, calming blemishes and supporting mature complexions. Emotionally it is used to ease stress, nervous exhaustion and restlessness. It also appears in foot and body blends for its fresh, cleansing scent.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face. Avoid on children under 2.
uses: Substitute for rose in love and self-love oils
Anoint a pink candle for friendship
Add to a heart-healing ritual bath
Blend into a facial oil for balanced skin
Diffuse with lavender for a peaceful home
Scent a love letter or charm sachet
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Palmarosa is affordable and rarely adulterated, but still check for Cymbopogon martinii var. motia; the related 'gingergrass' (var. sofia) smells quite different.
caution: Generally well tolerated and low risk, but geraniol can occasionally cause sensitization, so patch test on sensitive skin. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Palmarosa is best used on Fridays for Venus and in late summer, when the grass is harvested at its sweetest.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Patchouli Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried and lightly fermented leaves
aroma: Rich, dark and earthy, with a sweet, musty, wine-like depth that grows softer with age.
description: Patchouli is the deep, earthy base note of a thousand perfumes, and one of the few essential oils that actually improves with age, like a good wine. Its scent is grounding, sensual and unmistakable. In folk magic it is a powerhouse for money, lust and grounding.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally patchouli is one of the great money oils, used to anoint green candles, wallets, cash registers and business doors to draw steady prosperity. It is equally well known as a lust and attraction oil, and its earthy nature makes it excellent for grounding after ritual. In folk practice it is also used in fertility spells and, in some traditions, to banish or protect, since its strong scent is said to repel what is not welcome.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy patchouli is valued for skin care, especially for dry, cracked or mature skin and for the look of scars and stretch marks. Emotionally it is used to ground scattered thoughts, ease anxiety and reconnect with the body. It is a slow, steadying oil that also acts as a fixative to make other scents last longer.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face. Avoid on children under 2.
uses: Anoint a green candle or wallet for money
Add to a lust or attraction oil
Wear a dab to ground after ritual
Fix the scent of a sachet or potpourri
Blend into a balm for dry heels and elbows
Add to a business blessing floor wash
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Dark, aged patchouli is generally smoother and more prized than fresh, sharp batches. Indonesian patchouli is the classic source. Since a little goes a long way, a small bottle lasts years.
caution: Generally safe and non-irritating, though some people find the scent overwhelming or nauseating, so start small. May inhibit blood clotting; use cautiously if you take anticoagulant medication or have a bleeding disorder, and avoid before surgery. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Patchouli works best on Saturdays and Thursdays, in autumn harvest season, and in the earthy, grounding hours of late evening.
interactions: May add to the effect of anticoagulant drugs such as warfarin.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Peppermint Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the partially dried leaves and flowering tops
aroma: Intensely fresh, cooling and minty, with a sharp, sweet menthol bite.
description: Peppermint is a bright, electric oil that wakes up the mind and clears the air. In Greek myth the nymph Minthe was transformed into the mint plant, and mint has long been strewn and hung for freshness and protection. In folk magic it speeds spells along and draws both money and mental clarity.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally peppermint is used to cleanse spaces and raise the vibration of a room, especially when energy feels heavy or stagnant. A drop on a green candle or in a wallet oil is said to draw money and speed results. Its Mercury rulership ties it to communication, travel and study, and in folk practice it is used to sharpen psychic perception and to support healing spells for the body.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy peppermint is a classic for tension headaches, massaged in a diluted blend into the temples and back of the neck while avoiding the eyes. Its scent is widely used for nausea and travel sickness, and diluted into abdominal massage blends for digestive discomfort. It is a staple of steam inhalations and chest rubs for colds and congestion, and of cooling blends for sore muscles and tired feet.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid on the face and near the eyes. Never use on or near the face of infants and children under 6, and avoid entirely for children under 2.
uses: Diffuse during study for focus and memory
Anoint a green candle to speed money spells
Add to a cleansing spray for heavy rooms
Inhale from a tissue for travel nausea
Blend into a cooling foot or muscle rub
Add a drop to a travel protection charm
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Look for Mentha x piperita, not 'cornmint' (Mentha arvensis), which is cheaper and often passed off as peppermint. American Pacific Northwest and English peppermint are well regarded.
caution: Menthol can slow or stop breathing in babies and young children, so never apply on or near their faces and do not use at all under 2. Can irritate skin and mucous membranes; keep away from eyes. Avoid with cardiac fibrillation and G6PD deficiency. May worsen heartburn and acid reflux. Use sparingly in pregnancy; when breastfeeding, apply only after nursing and wipe off before the next feed, as it may reduce milk supply. Do not swallow the essential oil; keep it out of reach of children.
bestTime: Peppermint is best used in the morning or before study, on Wednesdays for Mercury, and in high summer when mint is at its most abundant.
interactions: Oral peppermint oil can affect drugs processed by CYP3A4 (such as cyclosporine) and antacids or acid reducers; topical and inhaled use carries little interaction risk.
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (named by Pet Poison Helpline): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Pine Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the needles and small twigs
aroma: Fresh, resinous and green, like a deep breath in a cold evergreen forest.
description: Pine oil captures the clean, bracing scent of the evergreen forest. As an ever-green tree, pine has long stood for resilience, renewal and life through the dark of winter. In folk magic it is a fierce cleanser and protector, as well as a herb of money and fertility.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally pine is used to cleanse and purify a home, especially at midwinter, and a few drops in a floor wash or spray are said to drive out negativity and return any ill will to its sender. It is a classic oil for Yule rites and for protection and exorcism blends. In folk practice it is also used to draw money and steady abundance, and to support healing, fertility and the courage to keep going through hard seasons.
