medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy pine is a respiratory oil, used in steam inhalations, diffusers and chest rubs for colds, coughs and congestion. It is a warming addition to massage blends for stiff muscles and achy joints, and its scent is used to revive tired minds and lift fatigue. Emotionally it is used to restore confidence and perseverance.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid on the face. Avoid on children under 6.
uses: Add to a Yule cleansing floor wash
Diffuse to clear a sickroom
Anoint a green candle for steady prosperity
Blend into a protection or return-to-sender oil
Add to a steam inhalation during colds
Blend into a warming chest rub
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Look for Scots pine (Pinus sylvestris) needle oil rather than generic 'pine oil', which may be a cheap industrial turpentine product. Buy small and fresh, as pine oxidizes quickly.
caution: Oxidized pine oil is a skin sensitizer, so store cold and tightly capped and discard old oil. Can irritate skin and mucous membranes. Avoid on children under 6 and use cautiously with asthma. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Pine is a winter oil, most potent from Samhain through Yule and Imbolc, and is best used in crisp morning air or at the solstice.
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (named by Pet Poison Helpline): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Roman Chamomile Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the flower heads
aroma: Sweet, apple-like and herbaceous, with a warm, honeyed, slightly fruity softness.
description: Roman chamomile is the gentle comforter of the oil cabinet, soft and sweet enough to be a favorite for calm and sleep. It is distinct from German chamomile, which is blue and more anti-inflammatory, while Roman chamomile is pale and especially soothing to the nerves. In folk magic it is a herb of peace, luck and gentle protection.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally chamomile is used to bring peace and calm to a troubled home, to invite restful sleep and to ease the spirit after upset. In folk magic it is also a luck and money herb, and gamblers once washed their hands in chamomile before playing. A drop in a ritual bath or a mist around the bedroom is said to soothe and protect, and it is often used in gentle spells for children's wellbeing, in very low dilutions or in the room rather than on the skin.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy Roman chamomile is used for nervous tension, irritability, restlessness and trouble sleeping, often in a bath or diffuser. It is a classic in gentle abdominal massage blends for digestive upset and menstrual discomfort, and in soothing blends for sensitive, irritated skin. Many aromatherapists consider it among the gentlest oils for use around older children.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 0.5-1% for face; 0.5% for children over 2.
uses: Add to a calming bedtime bath
Mist a bedroom for peaceful sleep
Anoint a gold candle for luck and money
Blend into a gentle tummy rub
Add to a peace oil for a tense household
Wash hands in a chamomile infusion before games of chance
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Check the label says Chamaemelum nobile (or Anthemis nobilis); German chamomile (Matricaria chamomilla) and Moroccan 'chamomile' (Cladanthus mixtus) are entirely different oils. Roman chamomile is moderately expensive, so very cheap bottles deserve suspicion.
caution: People with allergies to ragweed, daisies or other Asteraceae plants may react; patch test first. Generally very gentle on skin. Traditionally used sparingly in pregnancy. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Roman chamomile is best in midsummer when the flowers open in the sun, and it is most useful in the evening hours for calm and sleep.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Rose Essential Oil
latin: Rosa damascena (otto and absolute); Rosa centifolia (absolute)
partsUsed: Fresh petals and flowers, hand-picked at dawn
extraction: Rose otto is steam distilled from fresh petals; rose absolute is solvent extracted from the petals into a concrete, then washed with alcohol
aroma: Otto is fresh, delicate and honeyed like a living rose; absolute is deeper, richer and spicier, like a bouquet of full-blown roses.
description: Rose is the queen of oils and among the most precious, taking several thousand pounds of petals to make a single pound of otto. Two forms are sold: rose otto, steam distilled and prized in aromatherapy, and rose absolute, solvent extracted and loved by perfumers for its richer scent. In folk magic rose rules the heart, love, beauty and divine devotion.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally rose is used in love spells of every kind, from drawing romance to healing a broken heart and deepening self-love. A drop of diluted rose on a pink or red candle, in a ritual bath or on a heart-shaped charm is a classic working. In folk practice rose is also used for beauty and glamour magic, for peace in the home, for devotion to love goddesses, and for gently opening psychic and dream sight. Because it is so precious, many witches keep a small amount for their most important workings and substitute palmarosa or rose geranium for everyday spells.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy rose is considered one of the great emotional oils, used for grief, heartbreak, anxiety and low mood, mostly through inhalation or very low dilution massage. In skin care it is prized for dry, sensitive and mature skin. Rose otto is the form usually preferred in therapeutic aromatherapy, while rose absolute is mainly used in perfumery and for its scent.
dilution: Rose otto: maximum 0.6% (about 3-4 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin. Rose absolute: up to 2.5% for skin, though 0.5-1% is plenty. 0.5% for face. Avoid on children under 6. A single drop is often enough for ritual use.
uses: Anoint a pink candle for self-love
Add a drop to a love-drawing ritual bath
Blend into a glamour or beauty oil
Anoint a heart charm or love letter
Wear diluted as a devotional perfume
Inhale from a tissue during grief
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. True rose is very expensive; extremely cheap 'rose oil' is synthetic, heavily cut or rose geranium in disguise. Bulgarian and Turkish Rosa damascena are classic. Buying 3-10% rose in jojoba from a reputable distiller is an honest, affordable choice. Rose otto turns cloudy or solid in cool temperatures; warm it in your hands and it will return to liquid, which is a sign of genuine otto.
caution: Rose otto contains small amounts of methyleugenol, so keep it at 0.6% or less for regular use. Absolutes may contain traces of extraction solvent. Patch test on sensitive skin. Traditionally avoided in early pregnancy. Do not swallow the oil (culinary rosewater is a different product).
bestTime: Rose is at its peak in early summer when the roses bloom, and is best worked on Fridays for Venus, at dawn or by candlelight in the evening.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Rose Geranium Essential Oil
latin: Pelargonium graveolens (rose-scented cultivars, often Pelargonium x asperum)
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh leaves and stems
aroma: Sweet, rosy and green, with a minty, slightly citrus herbaceous edge.
description: Rose geranium is a scented pelargonium, not a true rose, but its leaves carry a remarkably rosy fragrance with a fresh green twist. It is affordable, versatile and balancing, making it a cornerstone of skin care and everyday love magic. In folk practice it is also a protective plant, grown on windowsills to guard the home.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally rose-scented geranium is used in love, fertility and friendship spells, and as an accessible substitute for rose in heart-centered work. In folk magic potted geraniums are kept on windowsills to protect the home and warn of approaching visitors, and the oil carries that protective quality into floor washes and doorway mists. It is also used for happiness and balance, especially when emotions swing between extremes.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy rose geranium is considered a balancing oil, used for emotional ups and downs, stress and nervous tension. It is a favorite in skin care for both oily and dry skin, and in massage and bath blends for premenstrual and menopausal discomfort. It also appears in natural insect-repelling blends.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face. Avoid on children under 2.
uses: Substitute for rose in love oils
Mist doorways for home protection
Add to a balancing ritual bath
Anoint a pink candle for friendship
Blend into a facial oil
Add to a fertility charm bag
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Look for Pelargonium graveolens or P. x asperum; Bourbon geranium from Reunion and Egyptian geranium are both well regarded. 'Rose geranium' and plain 'geranium' oil are often similar, so compare scents if you can.
caution: Can occasionally cause skin sensitivity; patch test on sensitive skin. May have mild hormonal effects in traditional use, so use sparingly in pregnancy. Use cautiously with diabetes medication. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Rose geranium is best used on Fridays and in summer when the plants are lush, with evening hours suiting love work and mornings suiting protection.
interactions: Cautioned with diabetes medication (mainly with oral use).
pets: Keep away from cats and dogs; geranium is toxic to pets if licked.

name: Rosemary Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the flowering tops and leaves; sold in chemotypes such as ct. cineole, ct. camphor and ct. verbenone
aroma: Fresh, herbaceous and camphoraceous, with a clean woody, slightly medicinal edge.
description: Rosemary is the herb of remembrance, worn by students in ancient Greece to sharpen memory and laid at graves and weddings alike. Its oil is bright and stimulating, waking the mind and clearing the air. In folk magic it is a powerful protector and purifier, often used as a substitute for frankincense.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally rosemary is used to protect the home, cleanse ritual spaces and banish negativity, and a long-standing folk substitute for frankincense in blessing and consecration. It is the classic oil for memory and remembrance: used in study spells, in honoring ancestors and the beloved dead, and in love and fidelity charms. In folk magic it is also used to restore health and youthful vigor, and a rosemary-scented bath before ritual is said to purify body and spirit.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy rosemary is used to sharpen concentration, ease mental fatigue and boost alertness, often diffused during study. It is a classic in warming massage blends for tired, stiff muscles and in steam inhalations for colds and congestion. It also has a long folk use in scalp and hair oils.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; avoid on the face. Avoid on or near the face of children under 6, and avoid entirely under 2.
uses: Diffuse during study for memory
Add to a protection floor wash
Anoint candles for ancestor remembrance
Use as a frankincense substitute in blessing oils
Blend into a scalp oil
Add to a warming massage blend
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Check the chemotype: cineole for respiratory blends, camphor for muscle blends, and verbenone for gentler skin care. Spanish, Moroccan and Tunisian rosemary are common and affordable.
caution: 1,8-cineole and camphor in rosemary can cause breathing problems in young children, so keep it away from their faces and avoid entirely under 2. Traditionally avoided in pregnancy, epilepsy and with high blood pressure. Can irritate sensitive skin. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Rosemary is best used in the morning hours and on Sundays, and is especially potent in spring for cleansing and at Samhain for remembrance.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Sandalwood Essential Oil
partsUsed: Heartwood and roots of mature trees
extraction: Steam distilled from the heartwood and roots; CO2 extracts also exist
aroma: Soft, creamy and sweetly woody, with a warm, milky, balsamic depth that lasts for hours.
description: Sandalwood is one of the most sacred woods on earth, used for centuries in temple incense, prayer beads and devotional paste. Its oil is deep, creamy and meditative, a base note that anchors any blend. Because Indian sandalwood was so heavily overharvested, choosing responsibly sourced oil is now part of working with it ethically.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally sandalwood is used to deepen meditation, raise spiritual vibrations and create a sacred atmosphere for prayer and ritual. In folk magic it is a classic wish oil: write a wish on paper, anoint it with sandalwood and burn it safely or keep it on the altar. It is also used for protection, healing, purification and for opening psychic and spiritual awareness, and its lunar rulership makes it well suited to full moon rites.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy sandalwood is valued as a calming, grounding oil for anxiety, nervous tension and restless sleep, especially when diffused or added to a bath. It is a treasured skin care oil for dry, sensitive and mature skin. Emotionally it is used to quiet mental chatter and settle the mind for rest or meditation.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face. Avoid on children under 2.
uses: Anoint a written wish before burning
Wear a dab for meditation and prayer
Consecrate prayer beads or a mala
Blend with rose for a devotional oil
Add to a calming bedtime bath
Blend into a nourishing facial oil
whereToFind: Buy from a supplier that lists the Latin name, country of origin, extraction method and ideally a batch GC/MS report. Choose dark amber or cobalt glass with an orifice reducer, and skip anything labeled 'fragrance oil', 'nature identical' or 'perfume oil'. Sustainability matters here. Indian sandalwood (Santalum album) is listed as Vulnerable by the IUCN after decades of overharvesting and illegal logging, so avoid wild Indian oil of unclear origin and look for certified plantation-grown S. album, including legal plantations in Australia. Australian sandalwood (S. spicatum) is harvested in Western Australia under regulated quotas and plantations; it is drier, sharper and lower in santalols, but a more sustainable choice for most uses. Note that 'West Indian sandalwood' or amyris (Amyris balsamifera) is not true sandalwood. Genuine sandalwood is costly, so cheap bottles are often synthetic or cut.
caution: Generally gentle and well tolerated, though rare skin sensitivity occurs; patch test. Traditionally used sparingly in pregnancy. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children. Please consider the environmental cost and buy only what you will use.
bestTime: Sandalwood is best worked in the quiet hours of evening and night, and on Mondays for its lunar rulership, at any time of year.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Star Anise Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried ripe fruit
aroma: Sweet, warm and intensely licorice-like with a faintly spicy edge.
description: Star anise oil captures the sweet licorice scent of the eight-pointed seed pod long prized in Chinese cooking and medicine. In folk magic the star-shaped pod is a symbol of luck and psychic sight, and the oil carries that same bright, opening energy. It is potent stuff, so a little goes a very long way.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally the eight points of the star anise pod are linked to luck and to opening the inner eye, so the oil is used in very small amounts in diffuser blends for divination, tarot reading and scrying. A single drop on a cotton ball tucked near the altar is said to sharpen intuition, and some practitioners add it to consecration oils for pendulums and spirit boards. In folk magic it is also a gentle protective scent, used to ward a working space before psychic work.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy star anise has been used, well diluted, in abdominal massage blends for bloating and sluggish digestion, and in chest rubs during colds for its warming quality. Its main component, anethole, is responsible for both the scent and many of the cautions, so it is used sparingly and for short periods rather than as an everyday oil.
dilution: Keep to 0.5-1% (3-6 drops per ounce of carrier) for occasional skin use; one to two drops is plenty in a diffuser; avoid on children under 6 and on sensitive or damaged skin.
uses: One drop in a diffuser blend before tarot or rune reading
Add to a consecration oil for divination tools
Anoint the corners of a dream journal (not the skin) for psychic dreams
Warming abdominal massage blend at 1% with sweet orange
Holiday simmer-style diffuser blend with orange and clove
Dab on a cotton ball in a luck sachet
whereToFind: Look for Illicium verum specifically and avoid anything unlabeled or labeled simply 'anise', which may be Pimpinella anisum. Buy steam-distilled oil in dark glass from a supplier who shares batch details, and skip synthetic 'licorice' fragrance oils.
caution: Anethole-rich oils should be avoided during pregnancy and breastfeeding, with endometriosis or estrogen-dependent conditions, and in children under 6. Can sensitize skin, especially once oxidized, so store tightly capped and cool. Never confuse with Japanese star anise (Illicium anisatum), which is poisonous. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Work with star anise in the cold months of late autumn and winter, ideally in the evening before divination or dreamwork.
interactions: Anethole is cautioned with anticoagulant medication (mainly with oral use).
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Sweet Orange Essential Oil
extraction: Cold pressed (expressed) from the fresh peel
aroma: Bright, juicy and sweet, like the moment you peel a ripe orange.
description: Sweet orange is the sunny, cheerful friend of the essential oil shelf: affordable, widely loved and easy to blend. Its golden scent has long been linked to joy, abundance and love in folk magic. It is one of the gentlest citrus oils and a favorite for beginners.
metaphysicalUses: Sweet orange is the classic oil for bringing sunshine into a working. Traditionally it is used in prosperity and abundance blends, in love and friendship oils, and in diffusers to lift heavy energy after an argument or a long winter. Add it to solar rituals, Midsummer celebrations and any spell where you want cheer and warmth to carry the intention. Anointing a yellow or orange candle with a few drops in carrier is a simple charm for good fortune and a happy home.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy sweet orange is diffused to ease nervous tension, low mood and restlessness, and it is a popular addition to bedtime blends for children over 6 and adults. Well diluted, it has been used in gentle abdominal massage for mild digestive upset.
dilution: 1-3% (6-18 drops per ounce of carrier) for body use; 1% for face; 0.5-1% for children 6 and over, and best diffused rather than applied for younger children.
uses: Diffuse with cinnamon and clove for a warm, abundant home
Anoint a gold candle for prosperity spells
Add to a love-drawing oil with vanilla and ylang ylang
Midsummer or solar sabbat diffuser blend
Cheerful room spray to clear stale energy
Bedtime diffuser blend with lavender
whereToFind: Buy from a reputable supplier that lists the botanical name, country of origin and extraction method; choose dark amber or cobalt glass, check for a recent pressing date since citrus oils oxidize quickly, and avoid anything sold as 'fragrance oil' or 'nature identical'.
caution: Generally considered non-phototoxic, but oxidized citrus oil can irritate and sensitize skin, so store it cold, tightly capped, and use within about a year. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Sweet orange shines in midwinter and around the summer solstice, and is best used in the morning to welcome the day's sunshine.
pets: Citrus oils (limonene) are toxic to cats: never apply to pets, store out of reach, and diffuse only briefly where pets and birds can leave the room.

name: Thyme Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the leaves and flowering tops
aroma: Strong, herbaceous and medicinal, warm and slightly spicy (the linalool type is softer and sweeter).
description: Thyme oil is a powerhouse distilled from the humble kitchen herb that has stood for courage and purification since antiquity. Several chemotypes are sold: red thyme (thymol-rich) is fierce and irritating, while thyme linalool (ct. linalool) is far gentler. Always check which one you have.
metaphysicalUses: In folk tradition thyme is the herb of courage, once given to knights and soldiers, so its oil is used in blends for bravery, confidence and standing your ground. It is a strong purifier: a drop in a cleansing floor wash or diffuser is traditionally used to clear a home of lingering negativity and illness energy. Old lore also ties thyme to the fairy folk, and some witches use a gentle thyme linalool in offerings or garden blessings.
medicalUses: Traditional aromatherapy uses thyme oil, very well diluted, in chest rubs and steam inhalations during colds and coughs, and in diffuser blends to freshen sickroom air. The gentler linalool chemotype is preferred for skin. Red thyme is generally reserved for diffusion and household cleaning blends.
dilution: Thymol-type (red) thyme: no more than 0.5-1% (3-6 drops per ounce) and best diffused; thyme ct. linalool: up to 2%. Avoid on children under 6, on the face, and on sensitive skin.
uses: Courage oil for job interviews or hard conversations
Cleansing floor wash for a sickroom or new home
Diffuse with lemon and tea tree during cold season
Very dilute chest rub with eucalyptus (linalool type)
Anoint a red candle for strength
Add to a protective sachet on a cotton ball
whereToFind: Check the label for Thymus vulgaris and the chemotype (ct. thymol, ct. linalool, ct. thujanol). Buy steam-distilled oil in dark glass from suppliers who list chemotype and origin, and avoid unnamed 'thyme oil' blends or fragrance oils.
caution: Thymol-rich thyme is a skin and mucous membrane irritant; never use undiluted or in the bath. Avoid during pregnancy, with high blood pressure, and in children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Work with thyme in early summer as the herb flowers, or in cold and flu season, ideally in the morning when you need courage for the day.
interactions: Thymol is cautioned with anticoagulant medication (mainly with oral use).
pets: Toxic to cats and best kept away from all pets.

name: Valerian Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried roots and rhizomes
aroma: Earthy, musky and pungent, often likened to old leather or damp socks, with a woody undertone.
description: Valerian oil is the famously smelly root of a plant revered for centuries as a calming, sleep-bringing ally. Its scent is challenging on its own, but a single drop deepens and grounds a sleep blend. It is a strong, earthy oil best used in tiny amounts.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic valerian root is used for protection, peaceful sleep and, oddly, love, since old lore says cats and lovers alike are drawn to it. The oil is added in very small amounts to sleep pillows (on a cotton pad tucked inside), to dream protection blends, and to calming oils for a quarrelsome household. Some practitioners use it in banishing and underworld work because of its earthy, rooty nature.
medicalUses: Traditional aromatherapy uses valerian oil in diffuser and bath blends for restlessness, nervous tension and difficulty falling asleep. Its strong scent means it is nearly always blended with sweeter oils such as lavender or mandarin.
dilution: 0.5-1% (3-6 drops per ounce of carrier) is ample for skin; one drop in a diffuser blend is usually enough; avoid on children under 6.
uses: One drop in a lavender and mandarin bedtime diffuser blend
Dream pillow charm on a cotton pad
Peace oil for a tense household
Grounding blend with vetiver after ritual
Add to a calming bath salt (dispersed in carrier first)
whereToFind: Valerian oil is less common and often expensive; look for Valeriana officinalis, steam distilled, in dark glass from a specialist supplier. Avoid 'valerian fragrance' and be wary of very cheap bottles.
caution: May add to the effect of sedatives, alcohol and sleep medications; avoid before driving. Avoid during pregnancy and breastfeeding and with young children. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Use valerian in the evening and late night, especially in autumn and winter when the roots are traditionally harvested.
interactions: May add to the effect of sedatives, sleep medications and alcohol.
pets: Cats are strongly attracted to valerian and can react unpredictably; keep bottles and treated items out of reach of pets.

name: Vanilla Essential Oil
extraction: Solvent-extracted absolute or supercritical CO2 extract from the cured beans; true vanilla cannot be steam distilled
aroma: Rich, warm, creamy and sweet, with a deep balsamic, almost smoky undertone.
description: Strictly speaking there is no true vanilla essential oil: real vanilla aromatics come as a CO2 extract or a solvent-extracted absolute from the cured beans. Most bottles sold as 'vanilla oil' are either an infusion of beans in a carrier oil or a synthetic fragrance, so read labels carefully. Genuine vanilla is thick, precious and deeply comforting.
metaphysicalUses: Vanilla is one of folk magic's favorite love scents. Traditionally it is added to love-drawing and self-love oils, used to sweeten relationships, and worn as a perfume to attract warmth and kindness. It also restores energy and comfort, so it appears in home blessing blends and in spells for a cozy, harmonious household. A homemade vanilla bean infusion in carrier oil works beautifully as an anointing oil if you cannot get the absolute.
medicalUses: Traditional aromatherapy uses vanilla's warm scent to soothe nervous tension, ease low mood and create a sense of comfort and safety, often in bedtime or relaxation blends. It is mostly used as a scent rather than for physical ailments.
dilution: Absolute or CO2: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for body use; 0.5-1% for face; patch test first and avoid on children under 6. Gently warm the bottle in your hand if the extract is too thick to pour.
uses: Self-love body oil with rose or ylang ylang
Anoint a pink candle for sweetening a relationship
Warm home blessing diffuser blend with sweet orange
Make a bean-in-carrier infusion as a gentle love anointing oil
Add to a comfort blend for grief or lonely nights
Prosperity perfume with benzoin and orange
whereToFind: Look for 'vanilla absolute' or 'vanilla CO2 extract' with Vanilla planifolia (or V. tahitensis) on the label and a price that reflects real vanilla. Labels such as 'vanilla oil', 'vanilla fragrance' or 'vanilla essential oil' at a low price are usually infusions or synthetics (vanillin). Store in dark glass; it may be thick or semi-solid.
caution: Absolutes may contain trace solvent residues, and vanilla can cause skin sensitization in some people; patch test before use. Avoid on children under 6 and during early pregnancy without professional guidance. Synthetic vanilla fragrance oils are not suitable for skin in the same way. Do not swallow vanilla absolute or CO2; use culinary extract for food.
bestTime: Vanilla is lovely all year but especially in the cold months and on Fridays, in the evening when love and comfort magic are best.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Vetiver Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the washed, dried roots
aroma: Deep, smoky, earthy and woody, like rich soil after rain with a hint of sweetness.
description: Vetiver is the deepest of grounding oils, distilled from the tangled roots of a tropical grass. Thick, dark and slow to evaporate, it is often called the oil of tranquility. A drop or two anchors any blend and makes the scent last.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally vetiver is used to ground scattered energy after ritual or a stressful day, and to root a spell firmly so it manifests in the physical world. In folk magic it is a money and luck oil, added to prosperity blends and dressed on green candles, and it is also used to break hexes and turn back ill-wishing. Anoint the soles of the feet (diluted) or the base of a candle to bring a working down to earth.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy vetiver is diffused or used in massage for nervous tension, restlessness and racing thoughts, and it is a common base note in sleep blends. It has also been used in skin care for its gentle, balancing qualities.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for body use; 1% for face; generally gentle, but avoid on children under 6 without guidance. It is very thick, so warm the bottle in your hand to help it flow.
uses: Grounding foot rub after ritual
Prosperity oil for dressing green candles
Hex-breaking and reversal blends
Sleep diffuser blend with lavender
Fixative to make a perfume last
Rooting a spell with a drop on the candle base
whereToFind: Look for Chrysopogon zizanioides or Vetiveria zizanioides, steam distilled, with origin listed (Haiti, Java and India are common). It should be thick and dark amber to brown. Buy in dark glass and avoid synthetic 'vetiver fragrance'.
caution: Generally well tolerated and non-irritating, but patch test if you have sensitive skin. Avoid during early pregnancy without professional guidance. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Vetiver suits autumn and early winter, and the evening hours when you need to settle and ground after the day.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Ylang Ylang Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh flowers, sold in fractions (Extra, I, II, III) or as Complete
aroma: Heady, sweet, exotic and floral, with creamy, fruity and slightly spicy notes.
description: Ylang ylang is distilled from the star-shaped yellow flowers of a tropical tree and is one of the most sensual scents in aromatherapy. In Indonesia its blossoms are traditionally scattered on the bed of newlyweds. It is powerful, so use it lightly or it can overwhelm a blend.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic ylang ylang is a love and attraction oil through and through. It is worn as a perfume to draw romance, dressed on red or pink candles for passion, and added to blends for self-love, confidence and sensuality. Traditionally it also brings peace to a relationship, soothing arguments and opening the heart. Pair it with sweet orange for joyful love or sandalwood for deep devotion.
medicalUses: Traditional aromatherapy uses ylang ylang to calm nervous tension, ease feelings of anger or frustration and lift low mood. It has long been used in hair care and in balancing skin care blends, and some aromatherapists use it in relaxation blends when the heart feels like it is racing from stress.
dilution: Up to 0.8% (about 5 drops per ounce of carrier) on skin to reduce the risk of sensitization; 0.5% for face; avoid on children under 6. Use sparingly in diffusers, as too much can cause headaches or nausea.
uses: Attraction perfume oil worn at the pulse points (diluted)
Dress a pink candle for self-love
Romantic diffuser blend with sweet orange
Calming bath blend for anger and frustration
Hair oil with a drop in jojoba
Harmony blend for a couple's altar
whereToFind: Check for Cananga odorata and the grade (Extra is the most fragrant and expensive, Complete is a good all-round choice). Buy in dark glass from suppliers who list origin, often Madagascar or the Comoros, and avoid synthetic 'ylang' fragrance.
caution: A known skin sensitizer, so keep dilutions at 0.8% or less and patch test; avoid on damaged skin. Strong scent can cause headaches or nausea if overused. Avoid on children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Work with ylang ylang on Friday evenings, in late spring and summer when love magic flows easily.
pets: Toxic to cats and dogs (ylang ylang is named by Pet Poison Helpline for cats): never apply to pets, store out of reach, and do not diffuse where pets or birds cannot leave the room.

name: Tea Tree Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the leaves and terminal branches
aroma: Fresh, sharp, medicinal and camphoraceous with a green, woody edge.
description: Tea tree is the workhorse of the first-aid kit, distilled from the leaves of an Australian paperbark tree. Its clean, sharp scent makes it a natural fit for cleansing and protection work. It is one of the most familiar essential oils, but it still needs care and dilution.
metaphysicalUses: Tea tree is not part of older European folk magic, but modern practitioners use it as a strong purifier and protector. A few drops in a cleansing spray or floor wash are used to clear a space of stagnant energy and illness, and it is added to healing spells and to protection blends for boundaries. Its sharp scent is also used to cut through mental fog before study or spellwork.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy tea tree is applied, diluted, to blemishes, minor cuts and scrapes, insect bites and fungal skin and nail complaints, and diffused or used in steams during colds. It is also a common addition to natural household cleaners.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for general skin use; up to 5% as a spot treatment on small areas for adults; 1% for face; avoid on children under 6 except under guidance.
uses: Cleansing room and altar spray with lemon
Purifying floor wash
Diluted spot treatment for blemishes
Healing spell candle dressing (diluted)
Cold season steam with eucalyptus
Protection blend for boundary work
whereToFind: Look for Melaleuca alternifolia, steam distilled, ideally from Australia. Buy small bottles, as tea tree oxidizes and becomes more irritating with age. Choose dark glass and avoid 'tea tree fragrance'.
caution: Oxidized tea tree oil is a common cause of allergic skin reactions, so keep it cool, capped and use within about a year. Never swallow it, including in homemade mouthwash; ingestion can cause confusion, loss of coordination and coma, especially in children. Avoid near eyes and ears.
bestTime: Use tea tree during cold and flu season, and at any time of day when a space or tool needs a deep, sharp cleansing.
pets: Highly toxic to cats and dogs, even a few drops on the skin or coat; never apply to pets.

name: Grapefruit Essential Oil
extraction: Cold pressed (expressed) from the fresh peel
aroma: Tart, zesty and sparkling, sweeter than lemon with a slightly bitter, fresh edge.
description: Grapefruit oil is pure sparkle, pressed from the peel of a fruit that only arrived in the 1700s in the Caribbean. Its uplifting scent is a favorite for mornings, motivation and fresh starts. Despite being a citrus, it is low in phototoxic risk when properly sourced.
metaphysicalUses: Modern practitioners use grapefruit to cleanse heavy emotional energy and invite optimism. It is added to purification sprays, morning ritual blends and spells for confidence, motivation and a fresh start. Traditionally citrus fruits are solar, and grapefruit brings that solar brightness in a crisp, clearing way, making it lovely for clearing envy or self-doubt from your aura.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy grapefruit is diffused for fatigue, low mood and mental sluggishness, and used in massage blends for a refreshing, invigorating feel. It is sometimes used in skin care for oily skin.
dilution: Cold pressed grapefruit: up to 4% for skin, but keep to 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for daily use; 1% for face; 0.5-1% for children 6 and over.
uses: Morning motivation diffuser blend with rosemary
Aura-clearing spray for envy or self-doubt
Confidence oil before a big day
Uplifting blend with vetiver to balance energy
Fresh start ritual on a new moon
Refreshing massage oil after a workout
whereToFind: Buy from a reputable supplier that lists the botanical name, country of origin and extraction method; choose dark amber or cobalt glass, check for a recent pressing date since citrus oils oxidize quickly, and avoid anything sold as 'fragrance oil' or 'nature identical'.
caution: Cold pressed grapefruit has low phototoxic potential, but stay within 4% on skin that will see sun within 12 hours. Oxidized citrus irritates skin, so store cold and use within a year. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Grapefruit is best in the morning and in late winter or early spring, when you want energy for new beginnings.
interactions: Grapefruit oil contains some furanocoumarins; if you take medicines with a grapefruit warning, ask your pharmacist before regular use.
pets: Citrus oils (limonene) are toxic to cats: never apply to pets, store out of reach, and diffuse only briefly where pets and birds can leave the room.

name: Spearmint Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the leaves and flowering tops
aroma: Sweet, fresh and green, softer and more candy-like than peppermint.
description: Spearmint is the gentler, sweeter cousin of peppermint, with a friendly scent many people know from chewing gum. It carries the bright, healing energy of mint without peppermint's strong menthol bite. That makes it one of the more suitable mint oils for sensitive noses.
metaphysicalUses: In folk magic mint is used for healing, money and love, and spearmint's soft sweetness makes it especially suited to gentle love and friendship blends. Traditionally it is also used to protect during sleep and to clear the mind, so a drop in a diffuser before study or spellwork sharpens focus. Add it to money-drawing oils with basil or to healing candles for someone recovering from illness.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy spearmint is inhaled or diffused to ease nausea and travel sickness, used diluted in abdominal massage for digestive discomfort, and applied to the temples (well diluted) for tension headaches. It is often chosen over peppermint for older children because it contains far less menthol.
dilution: 1-1.5% (6-9 drops per ounce of carrier) for body use, never above 1.7%; 1% for face and temples; can be used at 0.5-1% for children over 6; avoid on infants.
uses: Inhaler stick or tissue for travel nausea
Focus blend before study or ritual
Money-drawing oil with basil
Gentle love and friendship anointing oil
Healing candle dressing for someone convalescing
Fresh home spray with lemon
whereToFind: Check the label says Mentha spicata, steam distilled, in dark glass. Avoid oils that smell harshly of menthol (often blended with peppermint) and skip 'mint fragrance' oils.
caution: Contains carvone, which can irritate or sensitize skin; keep body use under about 1.7%, patch test and keep away from eyes. Avoid in large amounts during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Do not apply near the face of infants or young children. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Use spearmint in the morning and during spring and summer when mint is lush and fragrant.
pets: Mint oils are hazardous to cats and dogs; keep away from pets.

name: Neroli Essential Oil
partsUsed: Fresh flowers of the bitter orange tree
extraction: Steam distilled from the freshly picked blossoms
aroma: Honeyed, floral and citrusy, both delicate and radiant, with a faint green bitterness.
description: Neroli is distilled from the white blossoms of the bitter orange tree and is one of the most precious oils in perfumery. Orange blossom has traditionally crowned brides, linking it to love, purity and joy. A tiny amount is deeply calming and quietly luxurious.
metaphysicalUses: In folk tradition orange blossom is the flower of brides and new unions, so neroli is used in handfasting, marriage and commitment blends, and in spells for joyful, faithful love. It is also used to soothe grief and shock, to raise the spirits and to invite beauty and self-acceptance. Wear a drop in carrier as a ritual perfume when you want to feel radiant and calm at once.
medicalUses: Traditional aromatherapy uses neroli for nervous tension, anxious feelings and sleeplessness, often in very small amounts in massage or inhalation blends. It is highly valued in skin care for mature and sensitive skin.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for body use; 0.5-1% for face; avoid on children under 6. Many people buy neroli pre-diluted in jojoba because of its cost.
uses: Handfasting or anniversary anointing oil
Calming inhaler for nervous moments
Self-love and beauty perfume
Comfort blend for grief or shock
Luxury face oil at 0.5% in jojoba
Joyful love candle dressing
whereToFind: True neroli is expensive; look for Citrus aurantium flower oil, steam distilled, with origin such as Tunisia or Morocco. Very cheap 'neroli' is likely petitgrain, a blend or a synthetic. Pre-diluted 3-5% neroli in jojoba is a reasonable, honest option. Buy in dark glass.
caution: Not phototoxic and generally gentle, but patch test before use. Avoid on children under 6. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Neroli is lovely in spring when orange trees bloom, and in the evening for calming love and comfort work.
pets: Keep away from pets and do not diffuse in closed rooms with cats.

name: Benzoin Essential Oil
extraction: Solvent-extracted resinoid from the hardened tree resin, usually thinned with a solvent or carrier to make it pourable; it is not a true distilled essential oil
aroma: Warm, sweet, vanilla-like and balsamic, with a soft resinous depth.
description: Benzoin is not distilled at all: it is a resinoid made from the fragrant gum that weeps from Styrax trees. Thick and sweet like vanilla, it has been burned as incense and used as a perfume fixative for centuries. In magical practice it is prized for purification and uplift.
metaphysicalUses: Benzoin resin is one of the classic purifying incenses, and the resinoid carries that same work into oil blends. Traditionally it is used to consecrate tools, to cleanse and uplift a space, and in prosperity and success blends. Its warm sweetness also calms the mind before meditation, and some practitioners add it to astral travel and trance blends. It is a superb base for sealing a spell oil because it makes scents last.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy benzoin is used in balms for dry, cracked skin, in chest rubs and steams for coughs, and in warming massage for stiff muscles. Its comforting scent is also used for stress and loneliness. Friar's balsam, a traditional inhalation, is based on benzoin.
dilution: Up to 2% (about 12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 1% for face; avoid on children under 6. Check whether your product is already diluted in a solvent or carrier and adjust.
uses: Consecration oil for new tools and jewelry
Fixative base for spell oils
Prosperity oil with sweet orange
Purifying diffuser blend with frankincense
Balm for dry hands and heels
Calming blend before meditation
whereToFind: Check whether it is Siam (Styrax tonkinensis, sweeter, more vanilla-like) or Sumatra (Styrax benzoin, more balsamic). Ask what solvent or carrier is used to thin it; many are cut with ethanol, dipropylene glycol or benzyl alcohol. Avoid 'benzoin fragrance oil' and buy from aromatherapy specialists.
caution: A moderate skin sensitizer, especially Sumatra benzoin; patch test and keep dilution at 2% or less. Not for children under 6. Very sticky, so take care with fabrics. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Benzoin is best in the dark half of the year, especially around Yule, and at dusk when purifying a space for the night's work.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Sweet Marjoram Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried leaves and flowering tops
aroma: Warm, herbaceous and slightly spicy, with a soft, sweet, woody undertone.
description: Sweet marjoram oil carries the scent of a beloved kitchen herb that the ancient Greeks called the joy of the mountains. Legend says Aphrodite gave it its fragrance. It is a gentle, warming oil for comfort, grief and aching muscles.
metaphysicalUses: Traditionally marjoram was woven into wedding crowns and planted on graves to bring peace to the dead, so its oil is used both for happy unions and for soothing grief. In folk magic it protects the home and brings joy, and it is added to comfort blends for anyone mourning or lonely. A few drops in a diffuser are said to restore cheer to a sad house.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy sweet marjoram is a favorite massage oil for aching muscles, tension and menstrual cramps, and it is used in evening blends to quiet a busy mind before sleep. It is also used in inhalations for tension headaches.
dilution: 1-3% (6-18 drops per ounce of carrier) for body massage; 1% for face; 0.5-1% for children over 6.
uses: Comfort blend for grief and loss
Warming muscle rub with lavender and rosemary
Home protection diffuser blend
Wedding or handfasting blessing oil
Evening wind-down bath (dispersed in carrier)
Menstrual cramp massage over the belly
whereToFind: Make sure the label reads Origanum majorana, not Thymus mastichina (Spanish marjoram) or Origanum vulgare (oregano), which are very different. Buy steam-distilled oil in dark glass and avoid fragrance oils.
caution: Generally gentle, but avoid during pregnancy. Use cautiously with low blood pressure, as it is traditionally considered relaxing and lowering. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Sweet marjoram is best in summer when the herb flowers, and in the evening for comfort and rest.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Lime Essential Oil
partsUsed: Fruit peel (or whole fruit for distilled oil)
extraction: Cold pressed from the peel, or steam distilled from the whole crushed fruit
aroma: Sharp, tangy and sweetly zesty, like fresh-cut limes (distilled lime is softer and candy-like).
description: Lime oil is zingy, quick and cleansing, pressed or distilled from the small green fruit. Cold pressed and steam distilled lime behave very differently on skin, so it matters which one you buy. In modern practice it is a fast, bright purifier.
metaphysicalUses: Lime is used in folk magic to cut away hexes, jealousy and bad luck, often by slicing a fruit, but the oil carries the same sharp cleansing energy. Add it to banishing and uncrossing blends, purification sprays and protection oils, or diffuse it to clear a room after conflict. Its zest also brings energy and playful love, making it nice in friendship charms.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy lime is diffused for fatigue, mental fog and low mood, and added to steams during colds for its refreshing scent. Steam distilled lime is preferred for skin products.
dilution: Cold pressed lime is phototoxic: keep to 0.7% or less (about 4 drops per ounce of carrier) on skin that will be in sunlight within 12 hours. Steam distilled lime is not phototoxic and can be used at 1-2%. 1% for face; avoid on children under 6.
uses: Uncrossing and hex-breaking blend
Clearing diffuser after an argument
Energizing morning spray
Protection oil with tea tree and vetiver
Friendship charm with spearmint
Fresh cleaning spray
whereToFind: Check whether the oil is cold pressed or steam distilled; distilled is safer for skin. Look for Citrus aurantiifolia (or C. latifolia for Persian lime), dark glass and a recent date, and avoid 'lime fragrance'.
caution: Cold pressed lime is phototoxic: above 0.7% it can cause burns or dark patches on sun-exposed skin, so avoid sun and tanning beds for 12 hours after use. Oxidized citrus irritates skin; store cold. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Use lime in high summer and at midday, or whenever a fast, sharp cleansing is needed.
pets: Citrus oils (limonene) are toxic to cats: never apply to pets, store out of reach, and diffuse only briefly where pets and birds can leave the room.

name: Mandarin Essential Oil
extraction: Cold pressed (expressed) from the fresh peel
aroma: Soft, sweet and gently floral-citrus, mellower than orange with a delicate tang.
description: Mandarin is often called the children's oil because it is one of the gentlest and most comforting citrus oils. Its sweet, tender scent soothes rather than stimulates. In folk custom mandarins are gifts of luck and abundance at the new year.
metaphysicalUses: Mandarins are traditionally exchanged for good luck and abundance at the lunar new year, so the oil is lovely in prosperity and new year blends. Modern witches also use mandarin for family harmony, comfort and the inner child, adding it to home blessing sprays and peaceful bedtime rituals. Blend it with vanilla for sweetness or frankincense for a gentle, joyful consecration.
medicalUses: Traditional aromatherapy uses mandarin in calming blends for restlessness, nervous tension and sleeplessness, including for older children. It is often used in gentle tummy massage for mild digestive upset and in body oils during pregnancy (after the first trimester, with guidance) for stretch marks.
dilution: 1-3% (6-18 drops per ounce of carrier) for adults; 1% for face; 0.5-1% for children over 2, ideally diffused for younger children.

whereToFind: Buy from a reputable supplier that lists the botanical name, country of origin and extraction method; choose dark amber or cobalt glass, check for a recent pressing date since citrus oils oxidize quickly, and avoid anything sold as 'fragrance oil' or 'nature identical'.
caution: Very low phototoxic risk, though the green and yellow types carry slightly more; patch test. Oxidized citrus can irritate skin, so store cold and use within a year. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Mandarin is best in winter, especially around the new year, and in the evening for calm and comfort.
pets: Citrus oils (limonene) are toxic to cats: never apply to pets, store out of reach, and diffuse only briefly where pets and birds can leave the room.

name: Spikenard Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the dried roots and rhizomes
aroma: Heavy, earthy, musky and animalic, with woody, slightly sweet and valerian-like notes.
description: Spikenard, the ancient nard, is one of the oldest anointing scents in recorded history, prized in the ancient Near East and India. Distilled from the roots of a Himalayan plant, it is deeply grounding and quieting. It is also at risk from overharvesting, so source it thoughtfully.
metaphysicalUses: Spikenard has a long history as a sacred anointing oil, so it is traditionally used to consecrate altars, tools and people, and in devotional work. Its earthy calm supports deep meditation and peaceful sleep, and it is used to soothe grief and spiritual exhaustion. A tiny drop in a blend of frankincense and myrrh makes a timeless anointing oil.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy and Ayurvedic tradition, spikenard is used for nervous tension, restlessness and sleeplessness, often in a single drop added to a calming blend. It is also used in skin care for mature skin.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin, though one or two drops in a blend is usually plenty for its scent; 1% for face; avoid on children under 6.

whereToFind: Nardostachys jatamansi is listed as critically endangered in the wild. Look for suppliers who state cultivated or certified sustainable sources and provide origin (often Nepal or India). Buy small amounts in dark glass and avoid cheap 'nard' fragrances.
caution: Generally non-irritating, but avoid during pregnancy and with young children. May enhance the effects of sedatives. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children. Please use sparingly out of respect for this threatened plant.
bestTime: Work with spikenard at night, especially in the dark half of the year and during sacred or devotional rites.
interactions: May add to the effect of sedatives and sleep medications.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.

name: Helichrysum Essential Oil
extraction: Steam distilled from the fresh flowering tops
aroma: Honeyed, herbaceous and slightly spicy, with a dry, hay-like warmth and a curry-like hint.
description: Helichrysum is distilled from small golden flowers that keep their color long after drying, earning the names everlasting and immortelle. It is highly valued in skin care and is one of the more costly oils. Its symbolism of things that endure makes it a quiet magical treasure.
metaphysicalUses: Because its flowers never seem to fade, helichrysum is used by modern practitioners for healing old wounds, emotional as well as physical, and for spells of longevity, endurance and lasting bonds. It is added to self-forgiveness and inner healing blends and is lovely in ancestor work, honoring what endures. Anoint a gold candle with it for steady, lasting courage.
medicalUses: In traditional aromatherapy helichrysum is applied, diluted, to bruises, minor cuts and scars, and used in skin care for mature or damaged skin. It is also blended into massage oils for sore muscles and strains.
dilution: 1-2% (6-12 drops per ounce of carrier) for skin; 0.5-1% for face; can be used at slightly higher strength as a short-term spot application for bruises in adults; avoid on children under 6.
uses: Healing old wounds ritual oil
Scar and bruise balm with lavender
Ancestor altar anointing oil

Self-forgiveness meditation blend
Sore muscle massage blend
whereToFind: Look for Helichrysum italicum (Corsica, the Balkans and Italy are common origins); other species like H. gymnocephalum smell and behave differently. Because it is costly, it is often adulterated or sold diluted, so buy from trusted aromatherapy suppliers in dark glass and avoid fragrance oils.
caution: Generally gentle, but patch test. Traditionally avoided during pregnancy and with anticoagulant medications or before surgery. Do not swallow; keep the bottle out of reach of children.
bestTime: Helichrysum is best at midsummer when it flowers, and in the late afternoon sun for healing and renewal work.
pets: Keep away from cats, birds and small pets: never apply to animals, store bottles out of reach, and diffuse only briefly in a ventilated room pets can leave.
